titel: Sex-reversing frogs, and Europe’s rising rates of a deadly tick-borne disease

einzeiler: How climate change drives deadly tick-borne viruses and sex-reversing frogs in Europe
kurzfassung: This episode explores how climate change impacts two distinct animals in Europe: ticks spreading Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever and frogs undergoing temperature-driven sex reversal. International news correspondent Rich Stone details the spread of hyalomma ticks into cooler European regions due to warming temperatures. Evolutionary ecologist Veronica Bacconi explains how heat waves cause genetic female agile frogs to develop as males, threatening populations with extinction.
stichpunkte: Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever is a severe tick-borne disease with a high mortality rate of 20 to 25 percent in the Balkans.
Hyalomma ticks actively chase potential hosts over hundreds of meters and are spreading northward in Europe due to climate warming.
Kosovo maintains long-established tick surveillance and public education programs, advising people not to remove ticks with bare hands.
Unlike many turtles where cold temperatures produce males, fish and amphibians typically develop into males at high temperatures.
Agile frogs with XX chromosomes can develop testes when exposed to heat waves during the tadpole stage, becoming fertile sex-reversed males.
Offspring of sex-reversed male frogs show an increased sensitivity to heat and higher susceptibility to rhinovirus infections.
Theoretical models predict population collapse for such species within decades if climate warming continues without compensatory mechanisms.

clips.hook: Ticks that actively run after you
clips.text: Unlike typical passive ticks that wait on vegetation, hyalomma ticks actively pursue potential hosts and can run considerable distances after them.
Portugal recorded its first fatal case of Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever in 2024 amidst a recent emergence of the disease in Western Europe.

clips.hook: Turning into males during a heat wave
clips.text: Exposing genetically female frogs to a brief heat wave causes them to develop testes and transform into functional males.

clips.hook: A positive feedback loop toward extinction
clips.text: Offspring of sex-reversed frogs are themselves more likely to undergo sex reversal, creating a compounding cycle that skews sex ratios under warming climates.
Mathematical models incorporating field data suggest that affected frog species have only a few decades left before total population collapse if warming persists.

beschreibung:
First up on the podcast, Senior International Correspondent Richard Stone joins host Sarah Crespi to discuss how climate is pushing the disease-carrying tick Hyalomma marginatum out of its comfort zone. Stone reports from Kosovo, where the tick has long been endemic, on how surveillance can uncover hidden circulation—and help countries prepare before human cases appear.

Next on the show, researchers have long known ambient temperatures cause some species of amphibians to reverse sex. In the case of the agile frog (Rana dalmatina), genetically female frogs take on male characteristics at elevated temperatures—including the ability to sire offspring. Veronika Bókony, an evolutionary ecologist at the Center for Agricultural Science in Hungary, examined what happens to the offspring of sex-reversed agile frogs, which will probably make up more of the species’ population as the planet warms.
